title: Build performance & module graph
scopeHtml: How module structure, Gradle caching and annotation processing decide build time. Versions assumed: Gradle 8.x/9.x, AGP 8.x, Kotlin 2.x (verify exact numbers for your toolchain).

questions.promptHtml: How does splitting an Android app into modules make builds faster, and when does it make them slower?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: "Modularize for build speed" is a cliché answer. They want to know whether you understand the mechanism and its limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Gradle treats each module as a unit of work. A change recompiles only that module and modules that depend on it through compile-visible API. Independent modules compile in parallel, and unchanged modules are up-to-date or come from the build cache. It backfires when the graph is deep or wide-open (api everywhere), when modules are tiny so per-module overhead dominates, or when a hub module everyone depends on changes constantly.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Gradle's unit of up-to-date checking and caching is the task, and compile tasks are per module. In a monolith, one edit anywhere means compileDebugKotlin re-runs for the whole app module. Kotlin has its own incremental compilation, but it still works inside one big task with one classpath snapshot. In a multi-module build:

  • Only the edited module's compile task re-runs, plus downstream modules whose compile classpath ABI changed.
  • With org.gradle.parallel=true (or the configuration cache, which lets tasks run in parallel), independent modules compile concurrently, bounded by the longest dependency chain (the critical path).
  • Unchanged modules are UP-TO-DATE locally or FROM-CACHE from the build cache.

Costs: each module adds configuration time (AGP configures every project unless you use configuration-on-demand or the configuration cache), IDE sync time, and per-module task overhead (manifest merge, resource processing, lint, R generation).

monolith:   edit -> [ app: compile 100% ]
modular:    edit feature:a -> [a] -> [app]     (b, c, d untouched)
critical path = longest chain; parallelism cannot beat it

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// gradle.properties
org.gradle.parallel=true
org.gradle.caching=true
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Splitting by layer (ui, data, domain) so every feature edit touches all three and the critical path is long.
  • Hundreds of tiny modules: configuration and sync time grow faster than compile time shrinks.
  • Believing modularization alone helps when everything is exposed with api.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What bounds parallel speedup? -> The critical path and the number of cores/workers; a deep chain serializes.
  2. Does modularization help clean builds? -> Mostly via parallelism and remote cache hits, not via less work.
  3. How do you measure whether it helped? -> Compare build scan timelines and "avoided work" for a fixed set of benchmark edits before and after, not one-off timings.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer says "only changed modules rebuild". The senior adds critical path, ABI-driven invalidation, fixed per-module overhead, and says it is measured with scans.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams commonly report that incremental builds improve a lot while configuration time quietly climbs past 30-60 s after a few hundred modules, which is when the configuration cache becomes mandatory.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the phases of a Gradle build and tell me which phase you would look at for a 3-minute "nothing changed" build.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Diagnosing slow builds starts with knowing which phase is slow.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Initialization finds the projects from settings.gradle.kts, configuration runs every build script to build the task graph, and execution runs the selected tasks. A no-op build that is slow is almost never execution. It is configuration (scripts doing work, many modules, plugin resolution) or dependency resolution/up-to-date checks across huge inputs.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
1. Initialization: evaluates settings, includes projects, applies settings plugins, resolves plugin versions.
  2. Configuration: evaluates every build.gradle(.kts) (without configuration-on-demand), registers tasks, applies plugins (AGP creates variants here), wires dependencies. Eager tasks.create or afterEvaluate blocks and network or file I/O in scripts make this phase expensive.
  3. Execution: runs selected tasks and their dependencies, each checked for up-to-date or cache-hit first.

For a "nothing changed" build, task execution should show everything UP-TO-DATE. If wall time is still minutes, the build scan's "Performance" tab splits time into settings, configuration, dependency resolution and task execution. --profile writes an HTML report to build/reports/profile. Android Studio's Build Analyzer flags the same issues.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
./gradlew assembleDebug --scan
./gradlew assembleDebug --profile
./gradlew help --configuration-cache   # isolates configuration cost

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Timing only the first build; the daemon is cold and JIT is not warm.
  • Reading git/System.getenv/network in scripts at configuration time.
  • Optimizing compile tasks when 70% of time is configuration.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does AGP do its heavy lifting? -> Variant creation in configuration; compile and packaging in execution.
  2. What does the configuration cache skip? -> Configuration entirely on a cache hit; you go straight to execution.
  3. Why is ./gradlew help a useful benchmark? -> It does configuration with almost no execution, so it measures configuration cost alone.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE can name three phases. Senior ties each to symptoms, tooling (scan, profile, Build Analyzer) and which knob affects which phase.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team found 55 s of every build spent in configuration because a script shelled out to git rev-parse in each of 120 modules.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the effect of api vs implementation on recompilation. Why does api slow builds, and when is it still correct?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the most common cause of "one change rebuilds everything" and tests whether you understand compile classpath vs runtime classpath.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: implementation puts a dependency on the module's own compile classpath and on the runtime classpath of consumers, but not on consumers' compile classpath. api also exposes it at compile time. With implementation, an ABI change in the dependency invalidates only the direct dependent. With api, it propagates to everyone who can see it. Use api only when the dependency's types appear in your module's public signatures.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Gradle's compile avoidance compares the ABI of classpath entries, not their bytecode or timestamps. Kotlin does the same through classpath snapshots. If :core:network changes only a private function body, its ABI is unchanged and no consumer recompiles. If it changes a public signature:

:app -> :feature:home -> :core:data -api-> :core:network
                                  ^ ABI change here
implementation: recompile :core:network, :core:data   (home sees no network types)
api:            recompile :core:network, :core:data, :feature:home, :app

Rule: if a public function, property type, superclass or interface of module X mentions a type from Y, X must expose Y with api (or compile will fail). Otherwise implementation. Also, api widens what other modules can accidentally depend on, which erodes boundaries.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// :core:data/build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    api(projects.core.model)          // User appears in public signatures
    implementation(projects.core.network) // hidden from consumers
    implementation(libs.retrofit)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using api "so it compiles" instead of fixing the missing direct dependency.
  • Using api for the java-library compileOnlyApi/Android library cases without understanding transitive runtime.
  • Forgetting that annotation-processor classpaths see transitive api dependencies.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does implementation affect the APK? -> No, runtime classpath still includes it.
  2. A consumer needs a type from a transitive implementation dep? -> It must declare its own dependency; that is intended.
  3. How do you find over-exposed api deps? -> The Dependency Analysis Gradle plugin (buildHealth) reports "should be implementation" (verify current version).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The 3-YOE answer stops at "api is transitive". The senior explains ABI-based invalidation, the signature rule, and links it to boundary enforcement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A shared :core:model exposed everything with api, so each edit to a data class rebuilt 40 downstream modules; moving to implementation plus a thin :core:model-api cut that sharply.

questions.promptHtml: Distinguish up-to-date checks, incremental compilation and the build cache. Which one saves you on a fresh CI machine?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates conflate three different mechanisms.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Up-to-date checking skips a task when its inputs and outputs match the last local run. Incremental compilation lets a task that must re-run do less work, reusing its own previous state. The build cache stores whole task outputs keyed by an input hash and restores them, even from another machine. On a fresh CI agent, only the remote build cache helps, because there is no local history.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mechanism Scope Needs previous local state Granularity
Up-to-date Task Yes (build dir + history) Whole task
Incremental compile Inside task Yes (caches in build dir) Per source file
Build cache Task No Whole task output

The cache key hashes task type and implementation classpath, input properties, input file contents (not timestamps), and output names. A task is cacheable only if its type is annotated @CacheableTask. Inputs must be relocatable (relative path sensitivity) or entries will not hit across checkout directories. Local cache is stored in the Gradle user home; the remote HTTP cache typically accepts pushes only from CI.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// settings.gradle.kts
buildCache {
    local { isEnabled = true }
    remote<HttpBuildCache> {
        url = uri("https://cache.example.com/cache/")
        isPush = System.getenv("CI") == "true"
    }
}
// gradle.properties: org.gradle.caching=true

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Letting developers push to the remote cache, which poisons it with unreproducible outputs.
  • Custom tasks with undeclared inputs: cache hits with wrong content.
  • Absolute paths or timestamps as inputs, causing perpetual misses.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why would a cacheable compile task miss? -> Different JDK, different classpath ABI, absolute paths, or non-deterministic inputs.
  2. Does the cache replace incremental compile? -> No; a miss on a changed module still benefits from incremental compile locally.
  3. How to debug a miss? -> Compare build scans (task inputs diff) or -Dorg.gradle.caching.debug=true (verify flag in current docs).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "Gradle caches stuff". Senior separates three mechanisms and explains key composition and relocatability.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: CI jobs ran 18 min because each fresh agent rebuilt everything; enabling a push-from-main-only remote cache turned most PR builds into cache hits.

questions.promptHtml: What does the Gradle configuration cache store, what invalidates it, and why do plugins and build scripts break it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: In a many-module build, configuration time dominates incremental builds; this is the biggest lever and a common source of mysterious failures.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It serializes the result of the configuration phase, meaning the task graph and each task's state, and reuses it when nothing that configuration read has changed. That means no script evaluation at all on a hit. It is invalidated by changes to build scripts, gradle.properties, version catalogs, buildSrc, and any file, env var or system property read at configuration time. Things that hold a live Project or non-serializable objects in task actions break it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
On a hit, Gradle deserializes tasks into fresh objects and runs them, so task actions must not reference project, Task objects of others, or script-level state at execution time. Gradle records inputs read during configuration (files, env vars, system properties, even File.exists() checks since file API tracking arrived in 8.1, when the feature became stable). Reading the current git hash at configuration time is legal only through a ValueSource/providers.exec, which Gradle tracks.

Side effects: with the cache on, tasks can run in parallel including within one project, so undeclared inter-task dependencies that "worked" now race. As of the docs I read, the feature is the preferred mode since Gradle 9.0 but opt-in, with default-on planned for Gradle 10 (verify).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken: reads at configuration time, untracked, and captured Project in action
tasks.register("stamp") {
    val sha = "git rev-parse HEAD".execute().text   // not tracked
    doLast { println(project.name + sha) }          // Project at execution
}
// Fixed
val sha = providers.exec { commandLine("git", "rev-parse", "HEAD") }
    .standardOutput.asText
tasks.register("stamp") {
    val name = project.name
    doLast { println(name + sha.get()) }
}
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
org.gradle.configuration-cache.problems=warn

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving problems=warn forever and shipping a flaky cache.
  • Timestamps or random values at configuration time that invalidate every run.
  • Assuming the cache is invalid because "Gradle is flaky" instead of reading the HTML problems report.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How is it different from the build cache? -> It caches the task graph, not task outputs.
  2. What is Reusing configuration cache in output? -> A hit; Calculating task graph as no configuration cache is available is a miss.
  3. Why can it surface hidden race conditions? -> It enables fuller parallel execution, exposing missing task dependency declarations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE enables the flag. Senior knows the invalidation inputs, the ValueSource pattern, and the parallelism side effect.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After enabling it, a team saw random file not found failures because a custom task read another task's output without declaring the dependency.

questions.contextHtml:
A 90-module app turned on org.gradle.configuration-cache=true. Locally every run prints Calculating task graph as no configuration cache is available and configuration still takes 40 s. CI also fails once a week with an "Unable to serialize" error. Here is the convention plugin applied to all modules:

class AndroidLibraryConventionPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        val buildNumber = System.currentTimeMillis().toString()
        extensions.configure<LibraryExtension> {
            defaultConfig.buildConfigField("String", "BUILD_ID", "\"$buildNumber\"")
        }
        tasks.register("printBuildInfo") {
            doLast { println("${project.name} $buildNumber ${project.version}") }
        }
    }
}
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong and how would you confirm it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Turn the configuration cache off, it is unstable." That throws away the single largest incremental-build gain and ignores a deterministic root cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the cache entry ever get reused (second run, same tasks)? Is the miss on every run or only after edits? Which Gradle and AGP versions? Is the same plugin used on CI?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the flag on with problems=warn for local, but fix first; do not disable globally.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) currentTimeMillis() read at configuration changes the value every run and it feeds a task input (buildConfigField changes BuildConfig inputs), so every run differs. (b) project captured inside doLast is a serialization problem. (c) A third-party plugin is incompatible. (d) Version catalog or gradle.properties edited between runs (red herring if not).
  4. How I'd verify: Run twice with --configuration-cache and open the HTML problems report Gradle prints; it lists "invocation of Task.project at execution time". For (a), a scan or diffing two runs' inputs shows BUILD_ID changing; buildConfigField changes also recompile every consumer.
  5. Root cause: A time value at configuration time changes BuildConfig every run, invalidating compile tasks as well as defeating reuse, and project in doLast is not serializable.
  6. Fix: Short-term: capture values in locals (val name = project.name; val version = project.version.toString()), drop the timestamp from debug builds. Long-term: compute build ids in a dedicated cacheable task for release only, wired lazily (providers/ValueSource).
  7. Prevention: CI job that runs the build twice and fails on Calculating task graph the second time; plugin tests with Gradle TestKit.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set problems=warn globally on CI; warnings hide real corruption.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the timestamp is a product requirement in debug builds? -> Put it in a generated resource file written by a non-cached task, so only the final packaging task, not compile, depends on it.
  • Why did CI fail only weekly? -> Likely cache-entry eviction or a different agent image exposing the serialization; the root cause is the same.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite of a team that added a "build time" string to every debug BuildConfig. Incremental builds were full rebuilds for six months before anyone looked at the scan inputs.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: disables the cache and moves on.
  • Hire: finds the timestamp and project capture and fixes both.
  • Strong hire: also notes the downstream compile invalidation, proposes lazy ValueSource/task wiring and a twice-build CI check.

questions.promptHtml: Why is KAPT slow, how does KSP differ, and how does annotation processing in general hurt incremental builds?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Hilt/Room/Moshi codegen is often the biggest chunk of build time in a modular app.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: KAPT runs Java annotation processors by first generating Java stubs from Kotlin sources, which is an extra full pass, and its processors see a broad classpath so compile avoidance is weakened. KSP processes Kotlin symbols directly, without stub generation, and supports incremental processing. Android's docs say KAPT is significantly slower than KSP and recommend migrating where the library supports KSP.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
KAPT pipeline: Kotlin sources -> stub generation (Java stubs) -> javac with processors -> Kotlin compile. The stub step is paid even if no processor output changes. KSP hooks into the Kotlin compiler front end and hands processors a symbol model, with incremental tracking of which outputs depend on which inputs.

Impact in a multi-module build: every module with processors needs its own processing task. Dagger/Hilt aggregating processing means a change in one module can force reprocessing downstream; Hilt in particular has aggregating behavior across modules (see the Hilt chunk). A module that changes only a function body should not trigger processing; whether it does depends on processor incrementality (isolating vs aggregating).

Migration: Room, Moshi codegen and others support KSP; Dagger/Hilt had KSP support (Dagger KSP support became available and Hilt followed; verify the version you use because Hilt-on-KSP maturity has changed across releases).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
plugins {
    id("com.google.devtools.ksp")
}
dependencies {
    ksp(libs.room.compiler)
    // was: kapt(libs.room.compiler)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mixing kapt and ksp for the same library.
  • Applying kapt to every module "just in case".
  • Assuming KSP is automatically incremental for custom processors; the processor must declare dependencies correctly.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to find kapt cost? -> Build scan task timeline: kaptGenerateStubs and kapt tasks.
  2. Why does one processor in a module hurt more than expected? -> It adds a processing pass and can disable compile avoidance for annotated inputs.
  3. Isolating vs aggregating processors? -> Isolating outputs depend on one source element; aggregating depend on many, so any change reprocesses more.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "KSP is faster". Senior explains stubs, incrementality types and measures per-module processing time.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Removing kapt from 30 modules that only used it for one library moved 4 minutes off a clean build in a team's scan.

questions.promptHtml: What are non-transitive and non-constant R classes and why do they affect build time in a multi-module app?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: R class handling was a historic cause of whole-project recompiles.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: With transitive R classes, each module's R contained every resource from all its dependencies, so adding a resource in a leaf changed the R of every downstream module and forced recompiles. Non-transitive R classes make each module's R hold only its own resources, which keeps ABI changes local. Non-constant R fields in apps and tests avoid inlined constants, improving incrementality. Both are the default since AGP 8.0.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
In library modules, resource IDs are not final constants anyway (assigned at app packaging). Transitive R meant R.string.x could be referenced from a module that did not declare it, which also hid wrong dependencies. With non-transitive R, you must reference com.example.core.ui.R.string.x or set android:namespace correctly, which exposes true dependencies.

Non-constant R: app and test R fields are not static final, so Java compilation does not inline them and resource changes do not ripple through constant folding.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# gradle.properties (defaults on AGP 8.0+)
android.nonTransitiveRClass=true
android.nonFinalResIds=true

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Migrating late and fixing hundreds of R imports by hand; use the IDE refactor (Refactor > Migrate to Non-Transitive R Classes).
  • Giving every module an unnecessary resources folder; modules without resources skip resource tasks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does non-transitive R expose dependency bugs? -> A module can no longer use a resource it does not depend on.
  2. Do they help compose-only modules? -> Less, but string/dimen resources still matter.
  3. Where is namespace set? -> android { namespace = "..." } in each module.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows the flag. Senior ties the ABI mechanism and the dependency-hygiene side benefit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: One team on an old transitive-R project saw any strings.xml edit trigger 70+ module recompiles until the migration.

questions.promptHtml: How does Kotlin incremental compilation decide what to recompile, and what code patterns make it recompile more than necessary?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who only toggle flags from people who can reason about ABI and invalidation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Kotlin tracks the ABI of the module's own sources and classpath snapshots of dependencies. When a dependency's snapshot changes, it computes which classes use the changed members and recompiles only those, plus transitive dependents of changed signatures. Fine-grained snapshots are used for project modules and coarse-grained (class ABI hash) for external jars. Public API churn, inline functions, constants and giant files widen the blast radius.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
From the Kotlin docs: fine-grained snapshots record members and recompile only dependents of modified members; coarse-grained recompile all dependents of a class whose ABI changed, used for jars in the Gradle cache. Triggers of wider recompiles:

  • Changing a public const val or inline function body: these are inlined into callers, so callers recompile.
  • Changing a sealed hierarchy: when exhaustiveness in dependents.
  • Very large files or "util" classes referenced everywhere: any change touches every user.
  • Typealias or extension function changes in a widely imported file.

kotlin.build.report.output=file writes reports explaining why a build was not incremental. kotlin.incremental=false exists but only for diagnosis.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Hot: every module reads this
object Flags { const val TIMEOUT = 30 }   // const is inlined into callers
// Safer
object Flags { val timeout get() = 30 }   // callers recompile less on value change
kotlin.build.report.output=file
kotlin.build.report.file.output_dir=kotlin-reports

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting everything in one Utils.kt or one Constants.kt.
  • Making all declarations public when internal hides them from dependents' ABI.
  • Confusing task-level avoidance with Kotlin's file-level incrementality.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does internal help ABI? -> Yes, internal members are not part of the ABI consumers compile against (they are mangled in bytecode but not source-visible).
  2. Why recompile on inline function body change? -> The body is copied into call sites.
  3. Why do jars use coarse snapshots? -> Performance tradeoff since they change rarely.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "Kotlin is incremental". Senior reasons about snapshots, inlining, visibility and reads build reports.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A const val API version bumped daily recompiled 80 files across modules until it became a runtime-read property.

questions.promptHtml: What tools do you use to find out why a build is slow, and what do you look for in each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you diagnose with evidence instead of folklore.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Start with a build scan (--scan) for the timeline, phase breakdown, dependency resolution and cache hit/miss with reasons. Use --profile for a quick local HTML report, Android Studio's Build Analyzer for AGP-specific warnings (kapt, non-incremental tasks, configuration cache compatibility), and Kotlin build reports for incrementality. Compare the same benchmark edit before and after any change.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Tool Answers
Build scan Where time went, critical path, which tasks missed cache and why, dependency downloads
--profile Local, no upload, per-phase and per-task time
Build Analyzer Tasks that dominate, always-run tasks, GC share over 15% suggests heap increase
Kotlin build report Why Kotlin compile was not incremental
gradle-profiler Repeatable benchmarks with warm-up and scenarios
./gradlew :app:dependencies, dependencyInsight Resolution and who pulls what

Method: define scenarios (clean build, no-op, ABI change in leaf, non-ABI change in leaf, change in app). Run each several times, warm daemon, record median. Look at critical path, not just total CPU time, because parallel work hides in total.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --scan
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug --profile --offline
./gradlew :app:dependencyInsight --dependency okhttp --configuration debugRuntimeClasspath

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Comparing one cold run to one warm run.
  • Optimizing the longest single task when it is off the critical path.
  • Uploading scans of proprietary code to the public scan service; use a private Develocity server if policy requires.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to attribute time to a plugin? -> Scan "Performance" > configuration and plugin breakdown.
  2. What is "avoidance savings"? -> Time saved by cache hits and up-to-date, shown in Develocity (verify naming).
  3. How do you keep gains from regressing? -> Track median build time per scenario in CI and alert.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE opens a scan once. Senior builds benchmark scenarios, tracks them continuously, and reasons about critical path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team chased kapt for weeks; the scan showed 9 minutes of idle CI downloading dependencies with no cache.

questions.contextHtml: Product app, 140 modules, 70 engineers. Since a refactor two weeks ago, changing one line inside :core:common rebuilds about 60 modules and local incremental builds went from 40 s to 6 min. Developer complaints are rising; CI queue time is up 35%. The scan shows compileDebugKotlin re-running for 60 modules with the cause "classpath changed" and an ABI diff reported as changed. The change was an edit to a private function body. Nobody changed Gradle or AGP versions. A recent PR also added kapt to :core:common for a custom annotation.
questions.promptHtml: How do you find and fix the cause, and how do you prevent it returning?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more RAM and enable parallel." It treats cost as a resource problem when the cause is invalidation, not capacity.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the refactor change api/implementation? Is the edit really non-ABI (body only)? Is anything generated or time-stamped in :core:common? Is kapt new there? Is the build cache enabled for devs?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revert the kapt addition or the offending api declaration if the diff is small; announce a known issue so people avoid hot-patching :core:common in the meantime.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Many modules depend on :core:common via api chains, widening the set that sees the ABI. (b) kapt in :core:common generates stubs/sources whose output changes every run (non-deterministic), so the classpath ABI changes though the source edit was private. (c) Inlined const/inline change. (d) Another change like timestamped BuildConfig (red herring unless the diff shows it).
  4. How I'd verify: Two builds with a trivial body-only edit and compare scans' task input diffs for :core:common:compileDebugKotlin outputs. Run :feature:x:dependencies --configuration debugCompileClasspath to see how :core:common reaches consumers. Check the kapt tasks' outputs for unstable ordering. Use the Dependency Analysis plugin for api-vs-implementation findings.
  5. Root cause: Suppose the scan shows kapt output differs per run (e.g., embeds a generated timestamp or unordered map), changing the module's ABI jar hash each time; combined with api exposure in 60 modules, every consumer recompiles.
  6. Fix: Short-term: remove or fix the non-deterministic processor output (sorted, no timestamps) or move to KSP. Long-term: change api to implementation for non-signature deps; split :core:common into small API modules by theme so a change reaches few consumers.
  7. Prevention: A CI scenario benchmark ("body-only change in :core:common must recompile at most N modules") using gradle-profiler; lint/Konsist rule limiting api declarations; dependency-analysis check in PR.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not split :core:common into 30 modules in a panic; I would not turn off incremental compilation to hide it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if all consumers genuinely use its types in their signatures? -> Then api is correct; reduce churn by stabilizing the module (interfaces in one stable module, impl elsewhere).
  • What if the scan is unavailable on CI? -> Use --profile, Kotlin build reports and -i logs for "Task is not up-to-date because" lines.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite where a code generator wrote the date into a header comment; every build produced a new ABI jar hash and "incremental" meant "rebuild the world". Deterministic output fixed it in one line.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests hardware and flags only.
  • Hire: identifies api propagation and investigates with scans/dependencies.
  • Strong hire: also isolates processor non-determinism, adds a regression benchmark, and plans structural splitting without a risky big-bang.

questions.promptHtml: What properties of the module graph determine build performance, and how would you measure and improve them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: At scale, graph shape matters more than any flag.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Build time follows the critical path length (longest dependency chain), fan-in of hub modules (how many modules recompile when a hub changes), and fan-out (how many dependencies a module drags in). Wide and shallow graphs parallelize well; deep chains and giant hubs serialize and amplify changes. I measure depth, fan-in and the change-impact set per module and refactor hubs into stable, small API modules.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
good:   app -> features(10 parallel) -> core-api (small, stable)
bad:    app -> a -> b -> c -> d -> e (each needs previous compile)
hub:    :core:common used by 120 modules (fan-in 120)

Metrics: longest path length, fan-in per module, "blast radius" = number of transitive dependents, change frequency from git history. A hub with high fan-in and high churn is the worst combination. Fixes: invert dependencies with interface modules, extract stable abstractions, split by reason-to-change, use implementation, avoid feature-to-feature dependencies.

Tools: ./gradlew projects, the Dependency Analysis plugin, community graph plotters such as the module-graph assertion/graphing plugins (verify names), or a small script parsing dependencies output. Combine with git churn to rank.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Stable API module: interfaces only, rarely changes
// :core:analytics-api
interface Analytics { fun track(event: String) }
// :core:analytics-impl depends on api; features depend on api only

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Counting modules rather than shape.
  • Adding a "shared" dumping ground.
  • Ignoring change frequency: a hub that never changes is cheap.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do api/impl split help? -> Consumers depend on a tiny stable module; impl changes do not propagate.
  2. Is a shallow graph always better? -> Not if it requires duplicated code or huge modules.
  3. How to prevent drift? -> Automated graph assertions in CI (verify tool).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "keep modules small". Senior quantifies fan-in, depth, churn and ties them to targeted refactors.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hub with fan-in 120 and daily edits was the single largest contributor to CI minutes until it was split into stable API and volatile impl modules.

questions.contextHtml: A 110-module app has an 18-minute clean assembleDebug on CI (8 vCPU, 16 GB agents) and about 11 minutes on developer laptops. Leadership wants 8 minutes in one quarter without a rewrite. Facts from a scan: configuration 1m 40s; dependency resolution 50 s; kaptDebugKotlin tasks total 7 min CPU across 40 modules; Hilt aggregating tasks about 2 min; lint not in this task; Gradle JVM heap is 2 GB and GC is 22% of time. Parallel is on, configuration cache is off, remote cache is not set up.
questions.promptHtml: Lay out your plan, in order, with expected savings and how you would prove each.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Modularize more" or "buy bigger machines". Both ignore the measured breakdown.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 8 minutes for clean or typical PR builds? Are developers or CI the target? Do all jobs need clean builds? Can we use a remote cache? What are the heap/CPU limits on agents?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cheap wins first: raise heap (-Xmx6g, with MaxMetaspaceSize set), since GC at 22% exceeds the 15% guidance; enable configuration cache; remove android.enableJetifier if unneeded.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) kapt is the largest chunk (7 min CPU); migrating to KSP where supported. (b) No remote cache, so clean CI builds repeat work. (c) Configuration (1m40s) is pure overhead per run. (d) Dependency resolution 50 s is from dynamic versions or repository order (red herring if network is already cached).
  4. How I'd verify: Fixed benchmark scenarios with gradle-profiler (clean, no-op, leaf edit); compare scan timelines per change; Build Analyzer for GC share.
  5. Root cause: Time is spread across serial/ineffective work: heavy annotation processing, no caching across agents, and an untuned JVM.
  6. Fix: (1) Heap and GC tuning: expect configuration and compile GC overhead drop (measure). (2) Configuration cache: saves most of the 100 s on warm daemons, though not on cold CI unless the cache is restored. (3) kapt to KSP in modules where libraries allow; remove kapt from modules that no longer need it. (4) Remote build cache pushed from main, read-only for PRs: a clean PR build restores most compile tasks. (5) Pin dependency versions; put gradlePluginPortal() last in plugin repositories. Rough math: 18 min minus ~3 min (kapt to KSP) minus ~1.5 min (configuration/GC) leaves ~13 min cold; a cache hit rate of 60% on compile work gets close to the 8-minute goal on PR builds. State these as estimates to validate.
  7. Prevention: Budget per scenario tracked in CI; alert when median grows 10%.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not run clean builds on CI when cache restore suffices, and I would not push from PR jobs, which can poison the cache.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if Hilt does not support KSP in your version? -> Keep kapt only in the Hilt-using modules and minimize their number; verify current Hilt/KSP support.
  • What if the remote cache has a low hit rate? -> Look for non-relocatable inputs and non-deterministic outputs in scan input diffs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team bought faster agents and got 10% improvement; moving cache pushes to main-only and removing unused kapt got 45% for free.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: generic advice, no measurement.
  • Hire: ranks by the scan and covers KSP, cache, heap.
  • Strong hire: quantifies expected gains, separates cold CI from warm local, defines how to prevent regression.

questions.promptHtml: How do version catalogs and convention plugins affect build performance and maintenance, compared to buildSrc?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Build logic structure affects invalidation as much as app code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A version catalog (libs.versions.toml) centralizes coordinates in one typed place with no build-logic compile cost. Convention plugins in an included build (build-logic) share module setup. Unlike buildSrc, changing one file in an included build does not invalidate the entire build's task classpath, so fewer tasks lose cache hits. buildSrc changes invalidate everything.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
buildSrc is on the classpath of all build scripts and part of the build cache key, so editing it invalidates cached results and configuration cache broadly. An included build (includeBuild("build-logic")) compiles separately and Gradle can scope the effect better, but it still changes plugin classpath for applying projects, so keep convention plugins small and stable. A catalog edit invalidates the configuration cache (the catalog is a configuration input) but not compile tasks of unrelated modules unless the resolved versions change.

Benefits: consistent compile/target SDK, one place to apply implementation rules, standard test setup per module. Risk: a convention plugin that reads files or env at configuration time breaks the configuration cache (see earlier question).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// build-logic/convention/src/main/kotlin/AndroidLibraryPlugin.kt
class AndroidLibraryPlugin : Plugin<Project> {
    override fun apply(target: Project) = with(target) {
        pluginManager.apply("com.android.library")
        pluginManager.apply("org.jetbrains.kotlin.android")
        extensions.configure<LibraryExtension> { compileSdk = 35 }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Keeping all logic in buildSrc of a large repo.
  • Using Groovy ext blocks for versions.
  • Dynamic versions (1.+) which cause resolution checks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the catalog not slow builds? -> It is declarative metadata.
  2. Where do bundles help? -> Group dependencies that always travel together.
  3. How to enforce versions across modules? -> Catalog plus platform/BOM.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "catalog replaces constants". Senior covers buildSrc invalidation and CC interaction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A teams' every-PR cache misses traced to a small buildSrc edit that changed the plugin classpath hash for all tasks.

questions.contextHtml: A remote build cache was introduced two weeks ago. The expected CI time drop from 22 to 12 minutes did not happen; median is 20 minutes and hit rate in the cache dashboard is about 12% on PR builds. Two agent images exist (JDK 17 and JDK 21 on different pools). Jobs check out into /builds/<random-job-id>/repo. Last week an engineer's local build pushed to the cache by accident. Yesterday a flaky test failure only reproduced with cache hits. Cache storage is 200 GB with 14-day retention.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the hit rate low, and how do you make it trustworthy?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase storage." Storage is not the issue and it ignores correctness.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who pushes? Are cache keys identical for the same commit on two agents? Are miss reasons consistent? Which tasks miss most? Is the main branch warming the cache?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Disable pushes from non-CI clients; flush entries pushed by the engineer if corruption is suspected; keep PR builds read-only.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Two JDKs means different task implementation inputs, so entries are not shared across pools. (b) Absolute checkout paths in task inputs (custom or lint tasks without relative path sensitivity). (c) Non-deterministic task outputs (timestamps, generated IDs). (d) main does not run a warm-up build so PRs find nothing. (e) Retention (red herring at 14 days).
  4. How I'd verify: Run the same commit on two agents and diff the build scan's task inputs ("not cacheable"/miss reasons); look at the top missing task types; check that test tasks are cache-hit with correct inputs.
  5. Root cause: Typically a mix: JDK split, path-sensitive inputs, and cache never warmed from main.
  6. Fix: Standardize JDK toolchain (kotlin { jvmToolchain(17) }) across agents; mark custom task inputs @PathSensitive(RELATIVE); run a post-merge job on main that pushes; keep push CI-only. For the flaky test: check whether the test task declares all inputs (e.g., env var or a file it reads), since a cache hit replays a past result.
  7. Prevention: Hit-rate dashboard alert; job that builds the same commit twice on different agents and asserts hits.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not cache test tasks with undeclared inputs, and I would not trust local pushes.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if security forbids sharing the cache between untrusted PRs? -> Read-only for forks; push only from trusted branches.
  • What if cache is huge and slow to download? -> Cache only tasks whose recompute cost exceeds transfer cost; skip trivial tasks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team found a lint task embedding the absolute workspace path in its report input, so no two agents ever agreed on a key.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the cache server.
  • Hire: finds JDK/path/push policy issues.
  • Strong hire: also validates determinism, discusses test-task replay semantics, and adds hit-rate monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: A team proposes splitting :feature:checkout (about 90k lines Kotlin, 8 engineers) into :checkout:cart, :checkout:payment, :checkout:address, :checkout:summary, each with its own api/impl pair, to reduce incremental build time. Today an edit in checkout takes about 70 s to run on a laptop. The org already has 140 modules and configuration time is 55 s with the configuration cache off, sync takes 4 minutes. Checkout code is heavily interlinked via shared view models and models.
questions.promptHtml: Do you approve the split? How would you decide?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Smaller modules are always better" or "no, keep it simple" without data.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Where do the 70 s go (Kotlin compile vs resources vs kapt/Hilt vs dexing/install)? How coupled are the four areas by call graph? Do the teams have different owners? How often does each area change?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; first get data from a scan for a typical checkout edit.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Time is in Hilt/kapt aggregation or dexing, which splitting does not fix. (b) Real compile cost is Kotlin recompiling a large module; splitting helps only if edits stay in one piece. (c) Heavy coupling means edits propagate across the new modules, giving no gain and adding overhead.
  4. How I'd verify: Scan for 5 typical edits; Kotlin build report for what recompiled; dependency graph of internal packages (are cycles present?); git history to see co-change frequency across the four areas.
  5. Root cause: Unknown until measured; the decision depends on co-change coupling and where time goes.
  6. Fix: If most time is outside compile, fix that (KSP, configuration cache, avoid full APK install with Apply Changes). If compile dominates and edits are localized, split along the seams that rarely co-change, probably two modules rather than eight. Extract shared models into one stable module first. Enable configuration cache before adding modules so added configuration cost is not paid.
  7. Prevention: Module-creation checklist: owner, measured benefit, dependency direction; target budget for configuration time.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not create api/impl pairs for modules with only one consumer; the extra modules add configuration, sync and review overhead for no isolation benefit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if ownership is the real reason (different teams)? -> Ownership is a valid reason to split independent of build time, but then enforce boundaries with a stable API.
  • What if the split makes clean builds slower? -> Possible because of per-module overhead; weigh against incremental wins using the actual edit frequency.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite team split a 70 s module into six and ended at 65 s incremental, because every edit touched shared models that all six depended on, plus 20 s more sync.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: approves or rejects by opinion.
  • Hire: asks for a scan and co-change data.
  • Strong hire: weighs configuration/sync overhead, proposes a smaller split along low-coupling seams, and sets measurable success criteria.
